name: Burduna
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word. So, for example, the name of the language Yinggarda is pronounced as ying-ga-rda with stress on the ying. Do not put emphasis on later syllables as this sounds very unnatural in Yinggarda (English speakers might be tempted to say ying-ga-rda with stress on the middle syllable this would sound very strange to Yinggarda people). The same is true of Bayungu (pronounced BA-yoo-ngoo not ba-YOO-ngoo [capitals = bold in the source]) and other languages.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Burduna is not in the catalog. All four Glottolog 'stress/prosody' titles attached to burd1238 are spurious: each record carries language code = Burduna [bxn] 'computerized assignment from "rom"', triggered by the Romance corpus name C-ORAL-ROM; they concern prosodic-break annotation in Italian/French/Portuguese/Spanish speech and have nothing to do with Burduna (priority none). this search of works with stress in the title then looked for real Burduna sources: Austin's 1981 Lingua historical phonology, his 1988 PL classification paper, his 1983 'Southern Pilbara dictionaries', O'Grady-Voegelin-Voegelin 1966 (Talandji-Buduna section), Thieberger's 1993 handbook entry and the full text of the Wangka Maya 2007 Burduna Dictionary (recovered from the the Internet Archive ebook index, = Glottolog's Wangka Maya & Deak 2008) were all read and are silent on word stress. The only first-hand statement found is on Austin & Dench's Gascoyne languages website (yinggarda.org, 'Spelling'): 'In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word', declared to apply to all languages of the region including Burduna — a regional initial-stress generalization, not a Burduna-specific description. Still unread and worth acquiring: Austin's draft 'Reference grammar of the Kanyara languages' (high), Austin 1988a 'Aboriginal languages of the Gascoyne-Ashburton region' LTUWP 1 (medium), and the 1976/78 Burduna grammar sketch cited by Wangka Maya (medium). Everything downloaded is under with.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable (first vowel) of the word, stated as a general property of the Gascoyne region languages (Kartu: Yinggarda; Kanyara: Bayungu, Burduna, Thalanyji, Binigura; Mantharta) by the linguists who documented Burduna. No Burduna-specific stress statement was found in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (language names used as examples). The statement is a regional generalization on a public-education site, not a Burduna description; Burduna's own page on the same site gives phonological notes (long vowels, medial voicing contrast, unusual clusters) but nothing on stress. All Burduna-specific descriptions opened (Austin 1981, 1983, 1988a, 1988b; Wangka Maya 2007 dictionary; O'Grady, Voegelin & Voegelin 1966) are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statement found is a regional generalization ('Gascoyne region Indigenous languages.. In general, stress falls on the first vowel of a word.. The same is true of Bayungu.. and other languages') on the Austin & Dench site, whose language pages cover Yinggarda (ying1247), Bayungu (bayu1240) and Burduna (burd1238). It is first-hand from the linguists who documented Burduna but is not a Burduna-specific description; treat as fixed: initial syllable by regional attribution, pending Austin's Kanyara reference grammar. Burduna has two dialects (northern/southern, Austin 1988a); no dialect is specified.

Languages of the Gascoyne Region, Western Australia (website yinggarda.org), 'Spelling' page; the site's 'Languages and People' page says this information 'applies to all the groups and languages of the region', which it lists as Yinggarda, Bayungu, Thalanyji, Burduna, Binigura, Tharrgari, Thiin, Warriyangga and Jiwarli.
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-initial stress ('first vowel of a word'), asserted for all Gascoyne Region languages including the Kanyara group to which Burduna belongs, by the two linguists (Austin, Dench) who did the primary fieldwork. Caveat: it is a regional generalization illustrated with Yinggarda and Bayungu, not a Burduna-specific statement; no Burduna-specific stress statement was found in any open source (the 2007 Wangka Maya Burduna Dictionary, O'Grady-Voegelin-Voegelin 1966, Austin 1981/1983/1988 and Thieberger 1993 are all silent). Note Burduna has phonemic long vowels, including in non-initial syllables, which none of the read sources relate to stress.

sources.citation: O'Grady, G.N., C.F. Voegelin & F.M. Voegelin. 1966. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Six. Anthropological Linguistics 8(2), Kanyara subgroup pp. 103-108.
sources.quote: In both Talandji and Buduna, the inventory of linear phonemes is identical with that listed for Bailko-Pandjima. Vowel length is phonemic in Talandji but bears a very low functional load. In Buduna, vowel length is more productive ... Junctures are sentence-medial // (sustension) and +, and sentence-final / (rise) and # (fall and fade-out), in both dialects.
sources.note: Talandji-Buduna: phoneme inventory identical to Bailko-Pandjima, vowel length more productive in Buduna, junctures listed; no stress statement in the Kanyara section (the 'Word stress is on the initial syllable' line at scanned l. 7033 is Wanman, Wati subgroup).
